power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Due to the sensitive nature of the sociometric network data collected from minors and the risk of deductive disclosure within bounded school cohorts, the data cannot be made publicly available.

Access to de-identified data may be granted upon reasonable request for scientific purposes, subject to approval by the responsible institutional data access/ethics procedure and a data use agreement.
Dietary choices have a substantial impact on the environment and human health.

The consumption of meat in particular is associated with high greenhouse gas emissions, land and water use, and biodiversity loss compared to other products (Poore & Nemecek, 2018). 60 percent of the global food production's emissions is due to animal products (Xu et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The consumption of meat in particular is associated with high greenhouse gas emissions, land and water use, and biodiversity loss compared to other products <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Poore & Nemecek, 2018)</ref>. 60 percent of the global food production's emissions is due to animal products <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Xu et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, high meat intake, in particular red and processed meats, is associated with a higher risk of colorectal cancer, cardiovascular disease and mortality (Godfray et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In addition, high meat intake, in particular red and processed meats, is associated with a higher risk of colorectal cancer, cardiovascular disease and mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Godfray et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A healthy vegan diet leads to lower cholesterol, better insulin levels, and weight loss compared to a healthy omnivorous diet (Landry et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A healthy vegan diet leads to lower cholesterol, better insulin levels, and weight loss compared to a healthy omnivorous diet <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Landry et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, societies would benefit from a transition to diets lower in animal products, such as a vegetarian dietavoiding meat and fish consumption.
This is particularly true for Western societies in which people generally have sufficient access to food and tend to overconsume meat (Godfray et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This is particularly true for Western societies in which people generally have sufficient access to food and tend to overconsume meat <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Godfray et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Dietary habits are learned at a young age and difficult to change.
Parents have the largest influence on what children perceive as a 'normal' meal (Patrick & Nicklas, 2005), which in most developed countries includes meat.
text.formatted: Parents have the largest influence on what children perceive as a 'normal' meal <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Patrick & Nicklas, 2005)</ref>, which in most developed countries includes meat.

text.text: However, adolescence represents a window of change in which children start shaping their own identity and are influenced by what peers think, which may overrule parental norms.
Food choice is used by adolescents as an expression of autonomy (Neufeld et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Food choice is used by adolescents as an expression of autonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Neufeld et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, these new behaviors and identities can persist and shape their adult lifestyle (Sawyer et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Moreover, these new behaviors and identities can persist and shape their adult lifestyle <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Sawyer et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, to encourage vegetarianism and reduced meat consumption, adolescents are a particularly interesting target group.

In previous research, several key factors have been identified as predictors of adopting a vegetarian diet or reducing meat consumption, including meat availability, environmental awareness, health concerns, financial means, socio-demographic characteristics, emotions and attitude (Pechey et al., 2022; Stoll-Kleemann & Schmidt, 2017).
text.formatted: In previous research, several key factors have been identified as predictors of adopting a vegetarian diet or reducing meat consumption, including meat availability, environmental awareness, health concerns, financial means, socio-demographic characteristics, emotions and attitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Pechey et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Stoll-Kleemann & Schmidt, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These studies often conceptualize food choices as primarily driven by individual-level attributes.
Eating however, is a social activity, embedded in shared contexts.
Meals are consumed during social gatherings or used as opportunities to strengthen social bonds (Higgs & Ruddock, 2020; Séré de Lanauze & Sirieix, 2022).

text.text: On top of that, identities such as vegetarianism may be used in the social context to either fit in or stand out, or determine who one can get along with (Nezlek & Forestell, 2020; Séré de Lanauze & Sirieix, 2022).

text.text: Vegetarianism may also be influenced by peers and can be seen as a healthy food behavior.
However, vegetarianism differs from other (un)healthy consumption behaviors, as the drivers are also related to environmental and moral reasons.
Moreover, vegetarianism has different connotations and is not necessarily seen as something 'cool' or as a rebellion against the parental order.

Previous studies were contradictory on whether peers influence one another in their dietary habits (Pedersen et al., 2015; Salvy et al., 2011; Stok et al., 2016), and results on adolescent peer effects in sustainable food practices and vegetarianism specifically are lacking.

text.text: Therefore, the primary goal of this study is to assess whether adolescents in secondary education influence one another's adoption of a vegetarian diet.

A few studies have found cross-sectional similarities between social contacts specifically in terms of meat consumption behaviors and identities among adults (Severijns et al., 2023; Vandermoere et al., 2019).
text.formatted: A few studies have found cross-sectional similarities between social contacts specifically in terms of meat consumption behaviors and identities among adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Severijns et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Vandermoere et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, such similarities at one point in time do not reveal whether individuals become similar because they influence one another over time, or because they preferentially form relationships with others who are already similar.

From a social network perspective, these represent two fundamentally different processes: social influence, in which behaviors or identities change as a consequence of social interaction, and social selection, in which friendship ties are formed or maintained based on pre-existing similarities.
Failing to account for both processes simultaneously makes it impossible to disentangle the direction of causality underlying observed similarity between friends.

For example, adolescents may appear similar in their dietary identities either because vegetarian peers influence one another, or because adolescents who already are vegetarian are more likely to become friends in the first place.

As both processes can produce comparable cross-sectional network patterns, analyses that do not model network and behavioural dynamics jointly risk overestimating peer influence effects (Steglich et al., 2010).
text.formatted: As both processes can produce comparable cross-sectional network patterns, analyses that do not model network and behavioural dynamics jointly risk overestimating peer influence effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Steglich et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, studying social selection is important in its own right, as the composition of adolescents' peer networks may shape whether new dietary identities are socially reinforced, normalized, or marginalized over time (Valente, 2010).

text.text: One other study has modeled the co-evolution of friendships and animal product consumption behaviors over time, but it focused on a relatively small sample of 74 university students, rather than a large pool of adolescents (Severijns et al., 2025).

text.text: The secondary goal of this study is thus to assess social selection processes related to vegetarianism within adolescent friendship networks.
To fulfill the two goals of this study, we wield an advanced longitudinal social network analysis method called stochastic actor-oriented modelling for the co-evolution of network and behavior.
Two waves of data were collected among 1,372 secondary school pupils.

The approach allows us to simultaneously predict changes in the social network (friendships among school pupils) and changes in vegetarianism (versus omnivore), and thus control for confounding processes.
The results could inform future studies and interventions uncovering the social processes behind vegetarianism.
The social context can influence the maintenance and adoption of a vegetarian diet in various ways.

An important distinction is between (1) the persistence of social influence; whether food choices are adjusted in the short term, internalized into longer-term diets or reinforce maintenance of existing diets (Kelman, 1958; Rothman, 2000; Salvy et al., 2012), and (2) why people are influenced by others; their motivations (i.e., accuracy, affiliation and social support) (Cialdini & Goldstein, 2004; Deutsch & Gerard, 1955; Wing & Jeffery, 1999).

text.text: Persistence of social influence refers to whether influences are short-term, for example only in the presence of others or in a specific eating situation, or lead to longer-term changes in dietary habits that persists outside immediate social contexts, and potentially reinforce existing diets.
Rooted in Bandura's Social Learning Theory (Bandura, 1969), social modelling refers to individuals imitating the behaviors of others.
text.formatted: Rooted in Bandura's Social Learning Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bandura, 1969)</ref>, social modelling refers to individuals imitating the behaviors of others.

text.text: In the context of food behavior, this means adjusting one's food choices to align with those of surrounding others.
Modelling can refer to immediate imitation of others, but also to adopting beliefs and behaviors outside the presence of the model, through a video or perception of the food choice of another person.

Modelling is more likely when the individual wants to affiliate with or is similar to the eating partner, and for unhealthy snacks rather than healthy snacks or full meals (i.e., breakfast or lunch) (Cruwys et al., 2015; Romero et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Modelling is more likely when the individual wants to affiliate with or is similar to the eating partner, and for unhealthy snacks rather than healthy snacks or full meals (i.e., breakfast or lunch) <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cruwys et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Romero et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: However, individuals have also been found to imitate strangers ahead of them in line when choosing meals (Christie & Chen, 2018).
text.formatted: However, individuals have also been found to imitate strangers ahead of them in line when choosing meals <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Christie & Chen, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Adolescents are also susceptible to modelling effects, as shown by two studies on the amount and type of snacks eaten when modelled by a video or eating partner (Romero et al., 2009; Salvy et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Adolescents are also susceptible to modelling effects, as shown by two studies on the amount and type of snacks eaten when modelled by a video or eating partner <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Romero et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Salvy et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: While social modelling studies assume individuals to be influenced by eating in the presence of others, or by recently elicited beliefs about what others ate (e.g., through a video of another person eating), social networks can also influence longer-term and more private behaviors, such as the full-time adoption of a vegetarian diet.

This happens through internalization: Exposure to a social relation who is vegetarian or meat-reducing may encourage new beliefs (e.g., a more positive attitude on vegetarianism, or a perceived social norm that is more in line with vegetarianism) which become part of one's intrinsic motivation and then translate into a persistent change of behavior throughout all contexts (Kelman, 1958; Severijns et al., 2023).

text.text: It may also be the result of an exposure effect (Bornstein & Craver-Lemley, 2022): being close to a vegetarian exposes one to more vegetarian foods and restaurants, leading to new habits and a more positive attitude towards these foods and vegetarianism in general.

text.text: While experimental or longitudinal evidence on this internalization process is lacking, one study found correlational evidence for reducing animal product consumption (Severijns et al., 2023).

text.text: Rather than adopting new eating behaviors because of others, others may also reinforce existing eating behaviors.

According to Rothman (2000), behavioral maintenance is rooted in perceived satisfaction with the current behavior and outcomes of that behavior, which partially refers to related interactions with family and friends.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Rothman (2000)</ref>, behavioral maintenance is rooted in perceived satisfaction with the current behavior and outcomes of that behavior, which partially refers to related interactions with family and friends.

text.text: We may be more likely to maintain a certain diet when others do the same, have supporting beliefs, or even compliment us and therefore create a supportive environment, both emotionally and practically (Severijns et al., 2024; Wing & Jeffery, 1999).
text.formatted: We may be more likely to maintain a certain diet when others do the same, have supporting beliefs, or even compliment us and therefore create a supportive environment, both emotionally and practically <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Severijns et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Wing & Jeffery, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Social modelling, internalization, and reinforcement describe how individuals respond to others' eating behaviors, but they do not fully explain why people do so.
Social psychological research suggests three primary motivations underlying social influence: accuracy and affiliation (Cialdini & Goldstein, 2004; Deutsch & Gerard, 1955).
text.formatted: Social psychological research suggests three primary motivations underlying social influence: accuracy and affiliation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cialdini & Goldstein, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Deutsch & Gerard, 1955</ref>).

text.text: An additional motivation particularly for the social reinforcement of existing dietary identities is social support (Wing & Jeffery, 1999)).
text.formatted: An additional motivation particularly for the social reinforcement of existing dietary identities is social support <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Wing & Jeffery, 1999)</ref>).

text.text: The first motivation concerns the desire to behave in a correct, appropriate, or socially acceptable manner.
This process is often guided by descriptive norms, whereby individuals use the observed behavior of others as a reference point for their own conduct (Cialdini & Trost, 1998).
text.formatted: This process is often guided by descriptive norms, whereby individuals use the observed behavior of others as a reference point for their own conduct <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cialdini & Trost, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Particularly under conditions of uncertainty, observing what most people or socially significant others do provides a cognitive shortcut for determining appropriate behavior while reducing the effort required for decision-making (Cialdini & Goldstein, 2004).
text.formatted: Particularly under conditions of uncertainty, observing what most people or socially significant others do provides a cognitive shortcut for determining appropriate behavior while reducing the effort required for decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cialdini & Goldstein, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: In the presence of others, we may choose a restaurant meal based on what others choose, trusting their judgment.
When adopting a persistent vegetarian diet, we may be driven by information coming from others on the environmental consequences or how to cook a vegetarian meal (Severijns et al., 2023).
text.formatted: When adopting a persistent vegetarian diet, we may be driven by information coming from others on the environmental consequences or how to cook a vegetarian meal <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Severijns et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The second key motivation is affiliation: the desire to belong to or gain social approval of others.

This is also called impression management and is often guided by injunctive norms: beliefs about what others think we ought to do (e.g., depending on the context eating meat may be seen as bad, or as normal or masculine) (Cialdini & Trost, 1998).
text.formatted: This is also called impression management and is often guided by injunctive norms: beliefs about what others think we ought to do (e.g., depending on the context eating meat may be seen as bad, or as normal or masculine) <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cialdini & Trost, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: A reason for individuals to adjust their food choices and consumption is managing how they are perceived by others.
Consequently, what people eat can depend on which eating behaviors are viewed positively by social ties.

During adolescence in particular, food choices may serve important identity and status functions, leading adolescents to prefer products, brands, or eating practices that are socially valued among peers, regardless of their nutritional quality.
Indeed, there is evidence that an interest in healthy eating may sometimes be perceived as socially undesirable among adolescents (Stead et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Indeed, there is evidence that an interest in healthy eating may sometimes be perceived as socially undesirable among adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Stead et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Supporting this perspective, De la Haye et al. (2010) found that male adolescents who consumed larger amounts of junk food and unhealthy snacks were perceived as more popular within their peer networks.
text.formatted: Supporting this perspective, De la <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Haye et al. (2010)</ref> found that male adolescents who consumed larger amounts of junk food and unhealthy snacks were perceived as more popular within their peer networks.

text.text: Vegetarian diets could be perceived both positively and negatively, depending on the priorities of those one wants to affiliate with.
The increasing awareness of its health and environmental consequences may stimulate negative judgments about eating large amounts of meat.
A recent study found that in a sample of university students, those with a higher level of animal product consumption were less popular overall (Severijns et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A recent study found that in a sample of university students, those with a higher level of animal product consumption were less popular overall <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Severijns et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If this extends to adolescents, vegetarianism could be a favorable behavior.
In addition, the adoption of vegetarianism as an identity can be motivated by wanting to belong to a group in which the social identity is related to vegetarianism (Plante et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In addition, the adoption of vegetarianism as an identity can be motivated by wanting to belong to a group in which the social identity is related to vegetarianism <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Plante et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This also related to maintaining and pursuing a coherent self-concept.
We seek to avoid conflict within ourselves and therefore self-categorize into certain social groups.
We tend to be more susceptible to influence from individuals in the same group than from individuals that we categorize in another group (Cialdini & Goldstein, 2004).
text.formatted: We tend to be more susceptible to influence from individuals in the same group than from individuals that we categorize in another group <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cialdini & Goldstein, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Adolescents use food consumption or identities as an expression of a desired self-identity to others with the goal of fitting in or belonging to a certain peer group (Stead et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Adolescents use food consumption or identities as an expression of a desired self-identity to others with the goal of fitting in or belonging to a certain peer group <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Stead et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, social support plays an important role in both the adoption of a new, desired diet, and the maintenance of existing diets (Wing & Jeffery, 1999).
text.formatted: Finally, social support plays an important role in both the adoption of a new, desired diet, and the maintenance of existing diets <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Wing & Jeffery, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Research has indicated that vegetarian and vegans are sometimes judged or stigmatized by others, and therefore supportive environments facilitate the adoption and maintenance of those diets (Chuck et al., 2016; Jabs et al., 2000; Markowski & Roxburgh, 2019).

text.text: Social practices and cultural traditions also play role in this: eating with others who do not adhere to the intended diet and cultural events where meat is traditionally eaten pose a challenge to the adoption and maintenance of that diet (Chuck et al., 2016).

text.text: Previous studies on social influence on food behavior among adolescents have found that adolescent peers influence one another's consumption behaviors, like unhealthy snack and soft drink consumption (de la Haye et al., 2013; Wouters et al., 2010) and alcohol consumption (Leung et al., 2014).

text.text: A review showed that peer norms are associated with a multitude of food intake behaviors (e.g., consumption of fruit and vegetables, soft drinks and unhealthy snacks) (Stok et al., 2016).

text.text: More commonly, peer influence on adolescent eating behaviour has been found to operate in unhealthy directions.

Existing research suggests that peers tend to reinforce one another's consumption of snacks and energy-dense foods (Ragelienė & Grønhøj, 2020), whereas peer effects appear weaker for healthier dietary behaviours such as fruit and vegetable intake (Pedersen et al., 2015).

text.text: However, findings are not entirely consistent.
For example, Salvy et al. (2011) found that female adolescents consumed more energy from healthy snacks and less from unhealthy snacks when eating with friends compared to eating with their mothers.

text.text: Less studies have looked into social influence on the maintenance of vegetarian diets.

Focusing on university students, a recent study found no evidence of peer influence on meat consumption among friends, with influence processes emerging only from household members (Severijns et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Focusing on university students, a recent study found no evidence of peer influence on meat consumption among friends, with influence processes emerging only from household members <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Severijns et al., 2025</ref>).

text.text: An intervention study showed that involving family and friends in the process of dietary change (less animal products), made these dietary changes last longer (Severijns et al., 2024).
text.formatted: An intervention study showed that involving family and friends in the process of dietary change (less animal products), made these dietary changes last longer <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Severijns et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Altogether, adolescents may be susceptible to influence from their classmates, but evidence about vegetarianism in adolescent peer networks has yet to emerge.
The dependency between individuals' dietary practices and those of their social environment is not solely explained by social influence.
Personal characteristics determine who we connect with.
A characteristic may make us more or less likely to receive or initiate friendships.
In addition, people with similar characteristics (e.g., vegetarian/vegan or non-vegetarian) are more likely to select one another as friends.
It is generally known that people prefer to have friends who are similar to themselves (McPherson et al., 2001).
text.formatted: It is generally known that people prefer to have friends who are similar to themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(McPherson et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: There are several reasons for social selection related to dietary patterns: social identity, stigmatization and social practice.
Vegetarianism can be seen as a social identity.

On top of being an identity rooted in food practices, vegetarianism is associated with non-dietary factors, such as shared values and beliefs, including moral considerations related to animal welfare or the environment.
These beliefs serve as motivations for the dietary practice and align vegetarian identity with the concept of a social identity (Judge et al., 2022; Nezlek & Forestell, 2020).
text.formatted: These beliefs serve as motivations for the dietary practice and align vegetarian identity with the concept of a social identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Judge et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Nezlek & Forestell, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: According to social identity theory (Tajfel, 2010), individuals tend to categorize themselves and others into social groups based on characteristics they deem important.
text.formatted: According to social identity theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Tajfel, 2010)</ref>, individuals tend to categorize themselves and others into social groups based on characteristics they deem important.

text.text: This classification process leads individuals to define themselves both in relation to those who share similar characteristics and in contrast to those who do not (White et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This classification process leads individuals to define themselves both in relation to those who share similar characteristics and in contrast to those who do not <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(White et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In this context, shared vegetarian group identities can facilitate the formation and maintenance of friendships with those who hold similar identities, while distinguishing them from those who do not share these values (i.e., those with non-vegetarian identities).

If vegetarianism is perceived either as a positive or negative identity, this may mean that people are more or less likely to initiate friendships with vegetarians (lower popularity), regardless of their own dietary identity.
Similarly, being vegetarian may be associated with other traits, such as being more or less outgoing, and lead to initiating less friendships.
Furthermore, stigmatization of vegetarians and vegans by omnivores may be another reason for vegetarians to be less popular, and same-identity friendships to be more likely.
Vegetarian identities and practices may have adverse effects on social relationships with non-vegetarians.

Previous research provides evidence of stigmatization, skepticism, or even social exclusion experienced by vegetarians at the hands of non-vegetarians (Chuck et al., 2016; Jabs et al., 2000; Markowski & Roxburgh, 2019).
text.formatted: Previous research provides evidence of stigmatization, skepticism, or even social exclusion experienced by vegetarians at the hands of non-vegetarians <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chuck et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Jabs et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Markowski & Roxburgh, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: One explanation for this could be avoiding cognitive dissonance, a feeling of discomfort due to experiencing conflicting moral beliefs (Festinger, 1959), which arises when individuals' habits and moral beliefs regarding meat consumption do not align (Rosenfeld et al., 2020; Séré de Lanauze & Sirieix, 2022).
text.formatted: One explanation for this could be avoiding cognitive dissonance, a feeling of discomfort due to experiencing conflicting moral beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Festinger, 1959)</ref>, which arises when individuals' habits and moral beliefs regarding meat consumption do not align <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Rosenfeld et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Séré de Lanauze & Sirieix, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, practical considerations may also contribute to the formation of social ties among vegetarians.
Social activities involving food such as shared meals, dining out, or shopping for food may be less inclusive for individuals with minority dietary practices.
Restaurants and grocery stores often provide limited vegetarian options, which can make participation in shared eating situations more challenging for vegetarians (Chuck et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Restaurants and grocery stores often provide limited vegetarian options, which can make participation in shared eating situations more challenging for vegetarians <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chuck et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, vegetarians may be more likely to socialize and dine with others who share similar dietary preferences, thereby increasing opportunities for repeated interaction and friendship formation.

A recent study found that university students were more likely to select friends who shared the same dietary identity, specifically distinguishing between meat eaters and non-meat eaters (Severijns et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A recent study found that university students were more likely to select friends who shared the same dietary identity, specifically distinguishing between meat eaters and non-meat eaters <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Severijns et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: They also found that students with high levels of animal product consumption were less popular (less likely to be selected by others as friend).
Comparable evidence for adolescents remains scarce.

Existing studies on other food behaviors of adolescents have reported little evidence for friendship selection based on similarities in overall food intake (van den Broek et al., 2022) or junk food consumption (de la Haye et al., 2013).

text.text: At the same time, adolescents have been shown to select friends based on a range of other healthrelated characteristics and behaviors, including healthy lifestyles (Adams et al., 2022), body mass index (Simpkins et al., 2013), weight control behaviors (Simone et al., 2018), and alcohol consumption (Leung et al., 2014).

text.text: Vegetarianism may constitute a particularly salient basis for friendship selection because it extends beyond food choice and can function as a socially meaningful identity linked to ethical beliefs, lifestyle preferences, and social stigma.

Building on these theoretical considerations and prior evidence among university students (Severijns et al., 2025), we expect adolescents to preferentially form and maintain friendships with peers who share a similar vegetarian identity.

text.text: Peer processes are unlikely to operate independently of the size and structure of the social context in which they unfold.
Adolescents' peer networks are embedded in bounded school environments that shape opportunities for contact, repeated interaction, visibility, and social segmentation.

Classic network theory emphasizes that social ties are organized around shared foci of activity, such as classrooms, school routines, and peer groups, which structure who encounters whom and how often (Scott, 1981).

text.text: Building on this idea, research on adolescent network ecology shows that school organizational environments moderate the expression of tie-formation processes and generate variation in clustering, hierarchy, and segregation across adolescent peer networks (McFarland et al., 2014).

text.text: School size is one such contextual feature.

Smaller schools and year groups tend to provide more constrained and repeated opportunities for interaction, whereas larger schools offer broader choice sets but may also increase anonymity, social differentiation, and fragmentation of peer environments (Lee et al., 2000; McNeely et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Smaller schools and year groups tend to provide more constrained and repeated opportunities for interaction, whereas larger schools offer broader choice sets but may also increase anonymity, social differentiation, and fragmentation of peer environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Lee et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">McNeely et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: For vegetarianism, this contextual variation may be particularly relevant.
Vegetarianism is relatively uncommon in adolescence and may be socially marked in predominantly omnivorous peer environments.
Peer effects may therefore depend on whether vegetarian practices are visible, socially recognized, and supported within the local peer ecology.
In smaller year groups, repeated encounters and denser interaction structures may make dietary practices more visible and provide stronger conditions for social reinforcement and maintenance.
At the same time, smaller groups may be more homogeneous and provide less opportunity for minorities (such as vegetarians) to connect, be accepted, and spread behaviors to others.
In larger year groups, adolescents may have more opportunities to select friends from a broader pool, and be more exposed to heterogeneous behaviors.
However, peer environments in such larger cohorts may also be more fragmented, making minority dietary practices less consistently visible or reinforced.

We therefore consider cohort size not merely as a technical feature of the data structure, but as a potentially meaningful contextual condition shaping both friendship selection and peer influence processes.
The "Social Integration and Boundary Making in Adolescence" (SOCIALBOND) project is a longitudinal panel study of adolescents in the German federal state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
The present analyses are based on two survey waves, collected at the beginning of seventh grade (autumn 2018) and one year later at the beginning of eighth grade (autumn 2019).
Across both waves, 3,494 students from 37 schools participated in at least one wave of data collection.

School selection was not random but aimed to achieve balance across Germany's four main secondary school types: lower secondary schools (Hauptschulen), intermediate schools (Realschulen), comprehensive schools (Gesamtschulen), and academic-track grammar schools (Gymnasien).
Students in wave 1 were typically aged 12 to 13, while those in wave 2 were aged 13 to 14, reflecting the one-year panel design.
Gender distribution was nearly balanced, with 52.03% identifying as female in wave 1 and 52.76% in wave 2.
The response rate was 75.99% in wave 1 and increased to 80.48% in wave 2.

The study relies on sociometric network data, meaning that friendship ties were collected within clearly bounded grade-level groups, with all students asked to report their relationships with peers in the same cohort.
Therefore, prior to data collection, a complete roster of all students within each school cohort was generated for every participating school.
Using this roster, students could identify peers when responding to questions about their social network.
Each student was assigned a unique three-digit code that allowed them to nominate other students anonymously within their cohort.
Importantly, networks were measured at the level of entire grade-level, comprising all seventh or eighth graders within the school depending on the data collection wave.
Surveys were conducted on-site during regular school hours using audio-supported, computer-assisted self-interviews (CASI) on tablet devices.
This standardized, classroombased procedure ensured privacy, minimized interviewer effects, and facilitated consistent administration across schools.
Parental written consent was obtained in advance via materials distributed and collected by teachers.
Students with parental permission were then asked to provide active consent on the day of the survey.
To support participation, a €5 incentive was provided for each returned parental consent form, regardless of whether parental consent was granted or declined.
Vegetarianism was assessed using a single-item measure, asking respondents: "Which of the following applies to you?
I am...
Vegetarian, Vegan, None of the above."
Due to a low number of vegan respondents (wave 1 N=30; wave 2 N=24), the categories "vegetarian" and "vegan" were merged into a single group for the analysis.
As a result, the variable is coded dichotomously, distinguishing between those who identify as either vegetarian or vegan and those who do not.
Friendship networks were derived from a name-generator item administered to all students within a year group.
Participants were asked: "Who are your best friends in your grade?
Name up to 10 people from your grade."
Using the pre-generated grade-level roster, students nominated peers by entering their three-digit codes.
The resulting networks are directed and bounded within school cohort specific groups, capturing peer relationships across all classrooms within the same grade.

To analyze the co-evolution of friendship networks and vegetarianism during adolescence, we employ the R package RSiena (Ripley et al., 2026).
text.formatted: To analyze the co-evolution of friendship networks and vegetarianism during adolescence, we employ the R package RSiena <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Ripley et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: RSiena is a statistical tool specifically designed for the analysis of network dynamics using longitudinal data.

It is based on a collection of Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models (SAOM), which model network evolution as a process of repeated micro-steps where actors can change their ties or behaviors in response to the existing network structure and their own attributes.
The co-evolution models used in this study allow for the simultaneous analysis of changes in social networks and behavioral traits, such as vegetarianism.
These models assume that network ties and behaviors are interdependent, meaning that changes in friendship ties can influence the likelihood of adopting or maintaining vegetarianism, and vice versa.

The estimation of these models is conducted using the Method of Moments, which iteratively simulates the network and behavioral changes until the simulated data align with the observed data (Snijders et al., 2010; Steglich et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The estimation of these models is conducted using the Method of Moments, which iteratively simulates the network and behavioral changes until the simulated data align with the observed data <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Snijders et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Steglich et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Within each network micro-step of the simulations, an actor can add, maintain, or dissolve one outgoing tie, while during behavioral micro-steps, actors have the opportunity to adjust their behavior (here vegetarian versus not).
This is reflected in two distinct model parts: one where the friendship network formation is the dependent variable (network dynamics), and one where vegetarianism is (behavior dynamics).

To distinguish between processes governing the formation of new relationships and the persistence of existing ones, we estimated separate creation and endowment effects for all vegetarian-related network parameters.
Creation effects capture the propensity to initiate new friendship ties, whereas endowment effects capture the propensity to maintain existing ties once they have been established.
Likewise, separate creation and endowment effects were estimated for the behavioral influence parameters.

These distinguish whether the vegetarian identities of friends are associated with the adoption of vegetarianism among previously nonvegetarian adolescents (creation) or with the maintenance of existing vegetarianism over time (endowment).
This distinction enables a more nuanced assessment of whether peer processes primarily facilitate the emergence or the persistence of vegetarian diets.
This joint modeling framework allows for a nuanced understanding of how social relationships and dietary behaviors influence one another over time.

It also acknowledges that the network's overall structure serves as a social context that shapes the probabilities of individual behavioral changes and tie adjustments (Snijders et al., 2010; Steglich et al., 2010).
text.formatted: It also acknowledges that the network's overall structure serves as a social context that shapes the probabilities of individual behavioral changes and tie adjustments <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Snijders et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Steglich et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: To accurately estimate social selection and influence processes, SAOMs additionally account for endogenous structural tendencies that commonly characterize adolescent friendship networks, such as network density, reciprocity, transitivity, indegree popularity, outdegree popularity, outdegree activity, and network stability (out-jaccard similarity).

These effects capture fundamental network dynamics such as the tendency to reciprocate friendships, form clustered friendship groups, maintain stable ties over time, or concentrate ties among popular actors.

Controlling for these structural processes is essential, as similarities between friends may otherwise emerge from general network tendencies rather than from substantive selection or influence mechanisms related to vegetarianism (Ripley et al., 2026; Snijders et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Controlling for these structural processes is essential, as similarities between friends may otherwise emerge from general network tendencies rather than from substantive selection or influence mechanisms related to vegetarianism <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Ripley et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Snijders et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, same-gender and same classroom group within the grade cohort effects were included to account for well-established sources of homophily in adolescent friendship formation.

To estimate the co-evolution of friendship networks and vegetarianism across multiple school cohorts, we employed a multi-group stochastic actor-oriented model (SAOM) implemented in RSiena (Ripley et al., 2026).
text.formatted: To estimate the co-evolution of friendship networks and vegetarianism across multiple school cohorts, we employed a multi-group stochastic actor-oriented model (SAOM) implemented in RSiena <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Ripley et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This approach jointly estimates network and behavioral dynamics across several independent networks, allowing information from all included cohorts to contribute to the estimation of common effect parameters.

While the model allows network-specific rates of change, the effects governing friendship selection, peer influence, and endogenous network processes are assumed to be homogeneous across networks unless explicitly modeled otherwise.
This strategy was necessary because the prevalence of vegetarianism among adolescents was generally low, resulting in limited behavioral variability across time in several year groups.
RSiena models require observable change in both the dependent behavior and the network to estimate influence and selection processes (Stadtfeld et al., 2020).
text.formatted: RSiena models require observable change in both the dependent behavior and the network to estimate influence and selection processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Stadtfeld et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: If no students change their vegetarian status between waves, or if only a small number of transitions occur, the parameter estimates become unstable and the models fail to converge especially when analyzing each network separately.

For the multi-group analysis, we therefore included only grade-level networks in which at least one student became vegetarian and at least one student stopped being vegetarian between the two observation points.
In principle, all grade-level networks could be combined into a single multi-group model.
However, this pooled specification did not achieve acceptable convergence once betweennetwork heterogeneity was taken into account.

Score-type tests indicated that several parameters varied across year groups, and a pooled model including the required set of groupspecific dummy interactions became too complex relative to the available behavioral change in vegetarianism.
We therefore adopted a stratified multi-group strategy that retained as many networks as possible while reducing heterogeneity among the networks analyzed together.
Year group size was chosen as the stratification criterion for both methodological and substantive reasons.

Methodologically, multi-group SAOMs assume that non-rate parameters are common across groups unless heterogeneity is explicitly modeled, and strong violations of this assumption should be addressed either by modeling group-specific deviations or by analyzing more comparable subsets of networks (Ripley et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Methodologically, multi-group SAOMs assume that non-rate parameters are common across groups unless heterogeneity is explicitly modeled, and strong violations of this assumption should be addressed either by modeling group-specific deviations or by analyzing more comparable subsets of networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Ripley et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, network size and density are known to affect structural network parameters, including degree-related and triadic tendencies (Anderson et al., 1999; Faust, 2006).
text.formatted: In addition, network size and density are known to affect structural network parameters, including degree-related and triadic tendencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Faust, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Substantively, this decision is consistent with our theoretical argument that year group size constitutes a meaningful contextual condition for peer processes.

Based on this logic, we divided the networks into smaller year groups (n < 109; range = 67-106) and larger year groups (n ≥ 110; range = 110-173; see Figure A1 Online Appendix which illustrates the distribution of year group network sizes and the cutoff used for the size-based stratification).

text.text: The cutoff was chosen to create two empirically estimable and approximately balanced groups of year group networks.
Using a threshold of <110 students resulted in 10 smaller year groups and 12 larger year groups.
text.formatted: Using a threshold of <110 students resulted in 10 smaller year groups and 12 larger year groups.

text.text: Alternative nearby thresholds would have produced more imbalanced groups; for example, a cutoff around 99 students would have yielded 8 smaller and 14 larger year groups, whereas a cutoff around 119 students would have yielded 14 smaller and 8 larger year groups.
Thus, the selected cutoff balanced the aim of forming structurally meaningful size-based strata with the practical need to retain sufficient numbers of networks in both multi-group models.
To further ensure the robustness of the network analyses, a minimum network participation rate of 0.70 was required for each grade-level network.
Following simulation evidence on missing data in whole-network analysis, we used a 70% network-level response rate as a lower bound for inclusion (Kossinets, 2006).
text.formatted: Following simulation evidence on missing data in whole-network analysis, we used a 70% network-level response rate as a lower bound for inclusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kossinets, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Our threshold mitigates bias due to missing data and ensures that the observed network structure closely approximates the actual social environment.
Lower participation rates can distort estimates of core structural parameters and obscure peer influence and selection processes (Ripley et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Lower participation rates can distort estimates of core structural parameters and obscure peer influence and selection processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Ripley et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In this study, six out of the 37 school cohorts were excluded due to low participation rates (<0.70) across both waves.
text.formatted: In this study, six out of the 37 school cohorts were excluded due to low participation rates (<0.70) across both waves.

text.text: Notably, these cohorts also exhibited very limited behavioural change, making them unsuitable for dynamic modelling.
An additional nine cohorts were excluded because they did not meet the change criterion for vegetarianism (i.e., no new vegetarians and no drop-outs), leaving twenty-two school cohorts for analysis.
The final analysis sample consists of 22 school cohorts, 10 small and 12 large, comprising a total of 1,372 students.
Estimation was performed following standard convergence diagnostics: convergence ratios below 0.25 and all absolute t-statistics for deviations from targets below 0.10.
Missing data in network ties and behavioral variables were handled using RSiena's internal imputation procedure, which allows meaningful simulations despite incomplete data (Ripley et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Missing data in network ties and behavioral variables were handled using RSiena's internal imputation procedure, which allows meaningful simulations despite incomplete data <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Ripley et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For network ties, missing values in the first wave were imputed as absent ties (i.e., 0), based on the assumption of network sparsity.
In the second wave, missing ties were imputed using the last observation carried forward.
For behavioral variables, missing values were imputed using the most recently observed value; if unavailable, the next observation or the modal category was used.
These imputed values were treated as provisional and allowed to change dynamically during the simulation process.
This approach ensures that missingness does not bias parameter estimation while preserving the stochastic nature of actor-based decision processes in the model (Huisman & Steglich, 2008).

text.text: The models are split in two parts that are estimated simultaneously: network dynamics, explaining friendships, and behavior dynamics, explaining vegetarianism.
The results for structural parameters are consistent with established findings in adolescent network research (Snijders et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The results for structural parameters are consistent with established findings in adolescent network research <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Snijders et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In both models, outdegree (density) is negative and highly significant, reflecting the general sparsity of adolescent friendship networks.
Reciprocity shows a strong positive effect, indicating a robust tendency for mutual friendships.

Both models also reveal significant transitive reciprocity and transitive ties, highlighting the tendency for friends of friends to become friends in network formation, particularly in smaller grade-level networks.
Popularity effects were differentiated by indegree and outdegree.
Indegree popularity (i.e., receiving many nominations attracts more nominations) is consistently positive.
Activity effects, a student's tendency to make multiple nominations, are positive but small.
The out-jaccard similarity effect is positive and highly significant in both models, indicating substantial stability in friendship ties across waves.
This effect reflects adolescents' strong tendency to maintain existing friendships over time rather than forming new social connections.

Furthermore, same-gender and same-class homophily significantly predict tie formation in both school cohort types, reflecting the importance of structural boundaries, physical proximity and demographic similarity in adolescent social networks.
The results for social selection based on vegetarianism are mixed and primarily observed in larger school cohorts.
In smaller school cohorts, there is no indication of selection effects: neither maintaining nor initiating ties appears to be influenced by shared vegetarian identity between students.
In larger school cohorts, by contrast, selection effects are more pronounced.
A marginally significant negative effect was found for veggie alter creation, indicating a tendency for students to avoid initiating new friendships with peers who are vegetarians.
Additionally, a significant negative effect for veggie ego creation suggests that students who are vegetarians are themselves less likely to form new outgoing ties.
Conversely, the veggie ego maintenance parameter in larger grade-level networks is positive and significant, indicating that vegetarian students are more likely to maintain existing friendships.
The interaction terms for creation and maintenance between veggie ego and veggie alter are non-significant.
This lack of significant interaction implies that there is no support for a tendency to select friends with the same dietary pattern (both vegetarian or both omnivore).

In both smaller and larger school cohorts, the vegetarian linear shape parameter is negative and highly significant, indicating an overall tendency for vegetarian identity to remain rare over time when controlling for network and peer effects.

The total alter maintenance effect, which assesses whether having more vegetarian peers makes it more likely that an ego maintains their own vegetarian identity, differs between small and large grade-level networks.

In smaller school cohorts, this effect is positive and significant, indicating that students were significantly more likely to retain their vegetarianism if they were connected to more vegetarian peers.
In larger school cohorts, the total alter maintenance effect is not significant.

For total alter creation, which tests whether a higher prevalence of vegetarian peers promotes the initiation of vegetarianism, the estimates in both small and large school cohorts are non-significant.

Because the RSiena multi-group procedure assumes parameter homogeneity across the included grade-level networks, additional robustness analyses were conducted to assess and account for potential heterogeneity between networks.
Score-type tests were employed to evaluate whether model parameters differed systematically across grade-level networks.
Initial heterogeneity tests indicated substantial between-network heterogeneity in both the smaller and larger school cohort models (see Online Appendix Table A2 and A3).

text.text: In both the smaller and larger school cohort models, the global test of heterogeneity was significant (p < .001).

text.text: To account for this variation, we iteratively introduced school cohort specific dummy interactions for those parameters exhibiting substantial heterogeneity.

This procedure follows established RSiena practice for accommodating period-or group-specific deviations while retaining a pooled multi-group estimation framework (Lospinoso et al., 2011; Ripley et al., 2026).

text.text: After inclusion of these dummy interactions, the remaining heterogeneity was substantially reduced.

For the larger school cohorts model, the final global heterogeneity test was no longer statistically significant (p = .066), indicating that the assumption of parameter homogeneity across networks was sufficiently satisfied.
In the smaller school cohorts model, heterogeneity was markedly attenuated, with most effects no longer exhibiting significant deviations across cohorts.

Remaining heterogeneity was limited primarily to the nonsignificant veggie ego (creation) effect, whereas the substantive parameters related to vegetarianism behavior dynamics remained stable across school cohorts.
Importantly, the inclusion of heterogeneity controls did not meaningfully alter the substantive conclusions of the study.
The robustness models reported in the Online Appendix Table A1 produced highly similar estimates for the focal selection and influence parameters.

text.text: In particular, the positive maintenance-based peer effect in smaller school cohorts remained statistically significant, while the absence of significant vegetarianism creation effects persisted across both smaller and larger school cohorts.
Likewise, the pattern of weak or absent vegetarian homophily remained unchanged.
In larger school cohorts, findings still supported the lower friendship initiation and higher friendship maintenance tendencies of vegetarians.
Additional goodness-of-fit (GOF) diagnostics further supported the adequacy of the estimated co-evolution models.

text.text: Overall, the models reproduced the observed network structures and behavioral distributions reasonably well, suggesting that the estimated SAOM specifications adequately captured the underlying friendship and vegetarianism dynamics across grade-level networks.

This study provides new insight into how adolescent peer networks shape the development and maintenance of vegetarianism, a topic that has received limited empirical attention despite growing societal interest in plant-based eating among younger populations.

Using longitudinal sociometric network data and stochastic actor-oriented models, we were able to disentangle friendship selection and peer influence processes, thereby addressing an important limitation of prior cross-sectional research on dietary similarity among peers.
In doing so, the study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how adolescent dietary identities emerge and persist within everyday peer contexts.

Contrary to findings in the literature on homophily in a wide array of characteristics among adolescents (Fletcher et al., 2011; Rayner et al., 2013), and the finding that university students selected one another based on having the same (non-)meat-eater identity (Severijns et al., 2025), we found little evidence that adolescents systematically selected or maintained friendships based on shared vegetarian identity.
text.formatted: Contrary to findings in the literature on homophily in a wide array of characteristics among adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fletcher et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Rayner et al., 2013)</ref>, and the finding that university students selected one another based on having the same (non-)meat-eater identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Severijns et al., 2025)</ref>, we found little evidence that adolescents systematically selected or maintained friendships based on shared vegetarian identity.

text.text: In smaller grade-level networks, vegetarianism did not significantly shape friendship formation or maintenance.

In larger grade-level networks, vegetarian adolescents were less likely to initiate new friendships and marginally less likely to be selected by peers, although they were more likely to maintain existing ties over time.
This contradicts the findings by Severijns et al. (2025), who found that university students with a low animal product consumption were more likely to be selected as friends.
text.formatted: This contradicts the findings by <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Severijns et al. (2025)</ref>, who found that university students with a low animal product consumption were more likely to be selected as friends.

text.text: These different dynamics may reflect the different age groups, i.e., vegetarianism may be frowned upon among adolescents but seen more positively among college students.

The lack of support for homophily (becoming friends based on having the same dietary identity) indicates that other matching characteristics play a larger role than vegetarianism, such as gender or being in the same class group.

Together, our findings suggest that vegetarianism may function less as a basis for active friendship formation and more as a socially marked minority identity that can complicate broader peer integration in larger social environments.

This interpretation aligns with previous qualitative research indicating that vegetarians often experience subtle social distancing, social inconvenience during shared meals, or perceptions of norm deviation in meat-oriented social contexts (Chuck et al., 2016; Jabs et al., 2000; Markowski & Roxburgh, 2019).
text.formatted: This interpretation aligns with previous qualitative research indicating that vegetarians often experience subtle social distancing, social inconvenience during shared meals, or perceptions of norm deviation in meat-oriented social contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chuck et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Jabs et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Markowski & Roxburgh, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The findings may alternatively reflect an unobserved confounding characteristic, both associated with vegetarianism and the likelihood to initiate and attract friendships, such as extraversion or moralism.
The findings more consistently support peer reinforcement rather than peer diffusion mechanisms.
That is, vegetarian peers do not seem to make adolescents become vegetarian, but they may make it easier for adolescents who already identify as vegetarian to maintain this identity over time.
Adolescents in smaller school cohorts who were connected to more vegetarian peers were significantly more likely to stay vegetarian over time.
Importantly, however, we found no evidence that adolescents adopted vegetarianism because their friends were vegetarian.
This distinction is theoretically important because most longitudinal network studies of food-related peer influence have treated influence primarily as a general process of behavioural assimilation.
Our findings instead suggest that peer contexts may be more consequential for stabilizing already existing dietary identities than for initiating new ones.

In other words, vegetarianism among adolescents appears less characterized by contagion-like adoption processes and more by reinforcement dynamics that help sustain a relatively uncommon diet within supportive peer environments.
However, it also means that omnivorous diets are reinforced among peers, limiting the diffusion of more plant-forward, and thus healthy and climate-friendly, dietary habits.
This pattern may reflect the distinctive nature of vegetarianism compared to other adolescent health-related behaviors.

Behaviors such as alcohol consumption, smoking, or unhealthy snacking are often highly visible, socially shared, and embedded in routine peer interactions, making them particularly susceptible to diffusion processes within friendship networks (de la Haye et al., 2013; Leung et al., 2014; Stok et al., 2016; Wouters et al., 2010).

text.text: Vegetarianism, in contrast, may be less socially observable in everyday school interactions and depend on factors outside peer control, such as parental food practices, household meal structures, or food availability (Savage et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Vegetarianism, in contrast, may be less socially observable in everyday school interactions and depend on factors outside peer control, such as parental food practices, household meal structures, or food availability <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Savage et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Adolescents may therefore encounter structural constraints that limit their ability to adopt vegetarian diets even when they are socially exposed to vegetarian peers.

At the same time, maintaining a vegetarian diet in a predominantly nonvegetarian peer environment may require social affirmation and support, which could explain why reinforcement effects emerged primarily for maintenance processes.
The stronger reinforcement effects observed in smaller school cohorts further highlight the importance of network context.

Smaller grade-level environments may facilitate greater behavioral visibility, denser interaction structures, and more stable peer relations, thereby increasing opportunities for dietary identities to be socially recognized and reinforced.
In contrast, larger school cohorts may provide more fragmented peer ecologies in which minority dietary identities are less visible and less socially integrated.

The finding that vegetarianidentifying adolescents in larger school cohorts were less likely to initiate friendships may reflect anticipatory social costs or perceived norm divergence associated with non-meat eating in broader peer settings.

Taken together, these findings suggest that adolescent vegetarianism is socially embedded, but that peer dynamics primarily operate through mechanisms of reinforcement rather than behavioral diffusion.
This reinforcement means that vegetarianism is maintained through a supportive network but can also hamper the diffusion of more climate and health-friendly diets to omnivorous individuals.

More broadly, the study demonstrates the value of longitudinal sociometric network approaches for understanding vegetarianism development, as they allow researchers to distinguish whether adolescents become similar because they influence one another or because they selectively associate with similar peers.
This study makes several important contributions to the growing body of research on social influence, social selection and dietary practices.
First, by employing longitudinal sociometric network data, it moves beyond prior research that predominantly relied on cross-sectional survey designs or self-reported perceptions of peer influence.

Such approaches are limited in their ability to distinguish between social selection and influence processes and offer only restricted insights into causal dynamics (Snijders et al., 2010; Steglich et al., 2010).

text.text: In contrast, the stochastic actor-oriented models used here enable the simultaneous modeling of network and behavior co-evolution over time, providing a more robust analytical foundation.
Second, this study focuses on adolescence, a critical yet under-researched period for the development of long-term dietary identities, including vegetarianism.

Given that adolescence is marked by increased sensitivity to peer norms and a growing capacity for autonomous decision-making, it offers a crucial window into how dietary behaviors emerge and stabilize within social contexts (Bassett et al., 2008; Winpenny et al., 2017).

text.text: Despite these strengths, several limitations must be acknowledged.
Most notably, the data do not differentiate between dietary intentions and actual behaviors.

It is plausible that social influence operates first on intentions, which may not always translate into observable behavior due to external constraints, particularly in adolescence, where parental control over food choices remains high (Savage et al., 2007).

text.text: Furthermore, the measure of vegetarian identity captures self-identification only, without information on the frequency or consistency of dietary practices.
As a result, the variable may not reflect actual consumption.

This is particularly relevant in adolescence, where eating practices may be shaped not only by peers but also by parental food provision, household routines, availability of vegetarian options, moral and environmental concerns, health motivations, and broader developmental changes in autonomy (Savage et al., 2007; Stoll-Kleemann & Schmidt, 2017).
text.formatted: This is particularly relevant in adolescence, where eating practices may be shaped not only by peers but also by parental food provision, household routines, availability of vegetarian options, moral and environmental concerns, health motivations, and broader developmental changes in autonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Savage et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Stoll-Kleemann & Schmidt, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: It is therefore possible that peer influence first operates on attitudes, intentions, or self-presentations, which may not always translate into consistent dietary behavior.
Conversely, observed changes in vegetarianism may also reflect influences outside the friendship network captured here.

The binary nature of the variable further prevents us from detecting gradual or partial changes, such as reduced meat consumption, flexitarian practices, or shifts emerging through shared meals and peer routines.
This may have led to an underestimation of social influence effects.
Future research should aim to capture more fine-grained behavioral data, possibly through mixedmethods designs or diary-based food tracking in conjunction with sociometric assessments.
Lastly, the analytic strategy necessitated the selective inclusion of school cohorts in the analysis sample.
Only those with sufficient prevalence and variation in vegetarian identity were eligible for RSiena modeling.
While this approach was methodologically justified to ensure model convergence and validity, it may limit the generalizability of findings.
Future studies should consider strategies to model rare behaviors across broader samples, possibly by pooling across contexts or applying Bayesian extensions of SAOMs.
This study contributes to a deeper understanding of how adolescent peer networks shape and sustain vegetarianism.

By leveraging longitudinal social network data and actor-oriented modeling, we show that vegetarianism does not appear to be a strong basis for friendship homophily: adolescents were not more likely to form or maintain friendships with peers who shared the same dietary practice.

At the same time, vegetarianism was associated with friendship dynamics in larger year groups, where vegetarian adolescents were less likely to initiate new friendships but more likely to maintain existing ones.

Peer influence processes emerged mainly in relation to maintenance rather than adoption: having more vegetarian friends reinforced the likelihood of staying vegetarian, particularly in smaller year group environments.
Together, these findings suggest that vegetarianism in adolescence is socially embedded, but not primarily through simple diffusion or same-diet friendship selection.
Instead, peer networks may shape whether a relatively uncommon dietary practice is socially sustained, constrained, or stabilized over time.

To effectively promote plant-based eating during this formative life stage, future research and interventions must account for the relational and structural conditions under which dietary identities are negotiated and maintained.
